strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in media forensics: moving beyond opaque binary classification/segmentation masks toward interpretable, text-based explanations of facial manipulations.

Introduces a large-scale multimodal benchmark (MMTT) with 128,303 triplets (manipulated image, ground-truth mask, and descriptive text explanation) created across diverse manipulation techniques (GAN swapping, transformer inpainting, and diffusion inpainting).

The ForgeryTalker framework is well-designed, effectively combining a hybrid CNN-ViT Forgery Prompter Network (FPN) with an MLLM backbone (InstructBLIP) and a SAM-based mask decoder to simultaneously output masks and explanations.
The paper is clearly structured and provides extensive ablations validating the design choices of the FPN, loss functions, and prompt conditioning.
weaknesses: Evaluation of the generated explanations relies exclusively on surface-level automated overlap metrics (CIDEr, BLEU, ROUGE-L). These metrics are insufficient to measure factual correctness, faithfulness, and hallucination in descriptive forensic justifications; a rigorous human evaluation or factuality study is lacking.

Generalization capability is not evaluated outside the proposed dataset; there are no cross-dataset or out-of-distribution experiments (e.g., evaluating on existing benchmarks like FaceForensics++ or real-world deepfake media) to demonstrate whether the learned explanatory features transfer to unseen forgery generators.

The manuscript lacks qualitative visual case studies illustrating model predictions versus baselines, making it difficult to judge the qualitative nuance and visual grounding of the produced textual explanations.

Important ethical and dataset governance details are missing, including annotator compensation, IRB approval/consent protocols, and privacy considerations regarding the facial imagery sourced from CelebA-HQ and FFHQ.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in media forensics: moving beyond binary classification or pure segmentation masks toward interpretable textual explanations for detected facial manipulations.

The dataset creation effort is substantial, assembling 128,303 face forgery samples (spanning face swapping and GAN/diffusion inpainting) paired with human-written explanatory texts and segmentation masks.
The paper is clearly structured and well-motivated regarding the limitations of uninterpretable binary detection masks.
weaknesses: Marginal performance gains over the baseline: In Table 2, ForgeryTalker improves only marginally over base InstructBLIP on text generation metrics (CIDEr 21.5 vs. 20.9; BLEU-4 5.9 vs. 5.6; ROUGE-L actually drops from 24.8 to 24.3). In Table 3, adding FPN over 'w/o FPN' yields essentially flat performance on BLEU and ROUGE, showing that the proposed module provides very limited empirical benefit in practice.

Lack of faithfulness and hallucination evaluation: Relying purely on surface n-gram overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, CIDEr) is insufficient to evaluate whether the generated explanations are faithful, factually aligned with the visual anomalies, or hallucinated. No human evaluation or faithfulness/correctness probing is conducted.

Missing human subject ethics and annotation compensation details: The dataset relies on 30 annotators contributing thousands of hours of work, but the manuscript omits crucial details regarding annotator compensation, ethical review/IRB approval, demographic background, and inter-annotator agreement metrics.

Primary fit and orientation: The core methodology and task (facial deepfake detection, landmark extraction, CoordConv, SAM mask decoders) belong predominantly to computer vision / multimedia forensics, with minimal linguistic or computational linguistics depth beyond standard instruction fine-tuning.

Noticeable presentation and terminology inconsistencies: The dataset is inconsistently referred to as 'Multi-Modal Tramper Tracing' (MMTT) in the abstract, Section 3 heading, and Section 5.1, instead of 'Tampering Tracing', indicating a need for careful proofreading.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: moving beyond binary mask prediction in deepfake detection toward generating natural language explanations that justify why and where facial manipulation occurred.

Introduces a large-scale dataset (MMTT) comprising 128,303 manipulated facial images paired with both pixel-level masks and human-annotated textual descriptions across multiple manipulation types (GAN face-swapping, transformer-based inpainting, and diffusion-based inpainting).

The two-stage framework incorporating a Forgery Prompter Network (FPN) with coordinate convolutions reasonably leverages facial spatial priors to steer the multimodal language model toward salient regions.
weaknesses: Marginal performance gains over baselines: In Table 2, ForgeryTalker demonstrates very small improvements over the InstructBLIP baseline in language metrics (e.g., BLEU-1 31.1 vs. 30.6; BLEU-4 5.9 vs. 5.6; CIDEr 21.5 vs. 20.9) and actually underperforms InstructBLIP on ROUGE-L (24.3 vs. 24.8). On forgery localization, it does not outperform SCA (70.81 vs. 72.87 IoU).

Absence of human evaluation or fine-grained hallucination/factuality evaluation: N-gram overlap metrics (BLEU, CIDEr, ROUGE) are known to correlate poorly with the factual validity and faithfulness of detailed visual explanations. Evaluating whether the generated text accurately describes actual visual artifacts or hallucinates non-existent defects is critical for interpretability, but is missing.

Lack of out-of-domain / cross-generator generalization experiments: The evaluation is conducted solely on the in-distribution test split of MMTT (generated via E4S, MAT, and SDXL). There is no evaluation of how well the localization and textual interpretation transfer to unseen manipulation algorithms or real-world deepfakes in the wild.

Missing annotation ethics and compensation details: For a dataset involving 30 human annotators producing over 128k descriptions, essential information regarding annotator recruitment, wage/compensation rates, language proficiency, and IRB/ethical approval is completely omitted.

Notable typographical and editorial errors throughout the paper (e.g., alternating between 'Tramper Tracing' and 'Tampering Tracing' in the title/text/abstract; 'Quatitative Results' in Section 5.2; and unedited phrasing such as 'the resutls reveals that the discounting the unmodifed regions' in Section 5.3).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely task in multimedia forensics and multimodal NLP: moving beyond binary real/fake classification towards interpretable, grounded attribution reports that explain both where and why facial tampering occurred.

Presents Multi-Modal Tamper Tracing (MMTT), a large-scale dataset consisting of 152,217 samples across diverse manipulation paradigms (face swapping, attribute editing, diffusion- and transformer-based inpainting) with aligned masks and descriptive diagnostic texts.

Proposes a well-integrated baseline model (ForgeryTalker) that combines region prompting (FPN), multimodal feature extraction via a Q-Former, a SAM-based mask decoder for localization, and an LLM decoder for fluent attribution text generation.

Provides extensive experimental validation, including comparisons with both fine-tuned specialists and zero-shot LVLMs, cross-dataset zero-shot transfer evaluations (DQ_F++ and SynthScars), and detailed ablation studies on pre-training and module contributions.
weaknesses: Evaluation of generated attribution reports relies strictly on standard lexical matching metrics (BLEU, ROUGE-L, CIDEr). For forensic explanations, surface-level lexical similarity does not measure diagnostic correctness or hallucinated artifacts; task-specific factual precision/recall metrics, LLM-based evaluation, or human evaluation would provide much more reliable assessment.

Details regarding the human annotation pipeline are incomplete. For 152,217 samples annotated by 30 annotators with a 1-minute minimum observation constraint, the paper does not report inter-annotator agreement metrics, annotator recruitment/compensation details, or systematic verification of description consistency.

In Table 4, when using ground-truth region prompts (w/ FPN-GT), report generation improves markedly (CIDEr from 59.3 to 95.1), but forgery localization IoU drops notably from 73.67 to 66.90. This counterintuitive behavior is left unexplained.

Minor inconsistencies exist across tables; for example, the 'Full Set' performance in Table 9 reports an IoU of 71.00 and CIDEr of 56.90, whereas Table 2 and Table 4 report 73.67 and 59.3, respectively, without clarification of differing experimental setups.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in multimedia forensics: moving beyond binary detection and ungrounded segmentation to produce explainable natural language attribution reports paired with pixel-level localization.
Introduces MMTT, a large-scale multimodal dataset (over 152k samples across face swapping, face editing, and inpainting) with process-derived ground-truth masks and human-written diagnostic texts.

Proposes ForgeryTalker, a unified model incorporating a coordinate-aware Forgery Prompter Network (FPN), a multi-task pretraining objective, and dual decoders (SAM Two-way Transformer and LLM) that effectively bridges region prompting with textual report generation.

Extensive experimental benchmarking on MMTT and out-of-domain evaluation on external datasets (DQ_F++ and SynthScars), supported by informative ablations on the pretraining stages, prompter network, and data composition.
weaknesses: The annotation scale warrants clarification: 152,217 manual descriptions by 30 annotators with a minimum 1-minute observation time implies over 2,500 working hours per annotator; more details regarding the exact annotation workflow, compensation, and quality control throughput should be provided to ensure reproducibility and transparency.

Evaluation of generated reports relies exclusively on standard surface n-gram overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, CIDEr), which are known to correlate poorly with factual correctness in open-ended diagnostic generation; a targeted human evaluation or model-based factual faithfulness assessment is missing.

The current setup assumes all evaluated images are tampered, bypassing authentic images; without evaluating behavior on authentic faces, it remains unclear how prone the model is to hallucinating artifacts on genuine images.

Analysis of cascading errors from the Forgery Prompter Network to the downstream decoders is limited; when FPN makes false positive/negative region predictions, the extent to which the LLM hallucinates explanations is not quantitatively analyzed.

strengths: Introduction of a large-scale, high-quality multimodal benchmark: The MMTT dataset contains over 152,000 samples across multiple manipulation paradigms (face swapping, attribute editing, inpainting), pairing process-derived pixel-level masks with human-written diagnostic descriptions.

Well-motivated task definition: Moving beyond binary classification and pure mask segmentation toward joint localization ('Where') and natural language explanation ('Why') significantly advances the interpretability and trustworthiness of multimedia forensics.

Cohesive baseline architecture: ForgeryTalker effectively couples region prompt extraction (FPN) with dual decoders (SAM Two-way Transformer for dense mask prediction and an LLM for natural language generation) via a two-stage pre-training and fine-tuning strategy.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The experimental suite includes comparisons against both general LVLMs and specialized forensics models, zero-shot generalization checks on external benchmarks (DQ_F++ and SynthScars), and thorough ablations covering pre-training stages, prompt components, and manipulation types.
weaknesses: Superficial evaluation of generated explanations: The evaluation relies almost exclusively on surface n-gram overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE-L, CIDEr). For forensic attribution, standard captioning metrics fail to measure diagnostic factuality, hallucinated artifacts, or fine-grained attribution correctness. Adding attribute-level precision/recall or a dedicated human evaluation of report validity would strengthen the claims.

Limited linguistic diversity and template reliance: Based on the qualitative examples and word cloud, the annotated descriptions frequently exhibit repetitive syntactic patterns and vocabularies (e.g., 'asymmetrical eyebrows', 'not clear', 'skin tone'). A quantitative analysis of linguistic diversity and inter-annotator agreement is missing.

Robustness to in-the-wild degradations: The dataset is generated on high-quality aligned face datasets (CelebAMask-HQ and FFHQ). In realistic forensic scenarios, images undergo post-processing operations such as heavy JPEG compression, resizing, and social media re-encoding, but the paper does not assess how resilient the dual-decoder framework is to these common distribution shifts.

Details on annotation cost and verification: With 152k samples and an enforced minimum observation time of 1 minute per image pair across 30 annotators, the annotation effort represents thousands of person-hours. Clarification regarding total human effort, compensation, quality verification sampling rates, and whether automated filtering or templates were partially used would improve transparency.
